cycles.en_text_before_rewrite:
# The 20 Percent Charge Left the Stage. Oil Worries Remained.

In the oil market, the lead role changed in a single day. First came a proposed 20 percent charge on all cargo passing through the Strait of Hormuz. The next day, the proposal disappeared from the stage. Normally, that might have brought some relief to crude oil prices.

But the market reacted differently. Just after the charge plan disappeared, prices began to fall. Soon, however, they returned to a high level. It was as if the market were saying, “The talk about the charge is over, but the story of the strait is not.” The fee was gone, yet the worry remained. To understand the turn, we need to look at what the charge was meant to do.

### A fee meant to protect the strait

On July 13, Trump proposed a 20 percent charge on all cargo passing through the Strait of Hormuz. The idea was that those carrying the cargo would repay the money the United States spends to keep the strait safe. Crude oil also passes through it, so trouble with transport could push its price higher.

The stage was ready for a quick change, but the market still had another question.

### The charge leaves, but the danger stays

On July 14, Trump announced that the 20 percent plan would be replaced by trade and investment deals that the Gulf states were working on with the United States. He said the change came after “very productive discussions” with Middle Eastern leaders. The charge had left the stage, but that did not settle the market’s concern.

After the announcement, the rise in Brent crude futures briefly narrowed, but prices soon returned to nearly the high level seen before it; at the time of reporting, they were above $85 a barrel, up about 2.6 percent, because attacks between the United States and Iran continued, fears of a blockade at sea remained, and people still did not know whether tankers could pass safely—showing that the charge had left the stage, but the dangerous route remained the real lead actor, with its distant danger reaching gasoline prices and the cost of moving goods through crude oil.

## In one line

The fee disappeared in a day, but the danger around the Strait of Hormuz remained.

二十パーセントは退場した。それでも原油の不安は残った

原油市場で、主役が一日で交代しました。最初に登場したのは、ホルムズ海峡を通る貨物への二十パーセントの償還料です。ところが翌日、この案は舞台から消えました。普通なら、原油価格もひと安心しそうです。

しかし、原油市場の反応は少し違いました。料金案が消えた直後に、価格は下がりかけました。ところがすぐに、高い水準へ戻ったのです。まるで市場が、「料金の話は終わっても、海峡の話は終わっていません」と見ていたようでした。

始まりは七月十三日です。トランプ氏は、ホルムズ海峡を通るすべての貨物に、二十パーセントを求める案を示しました。アメリカが海峡の安全を守るために使う費用を、貨物を運ぶ側に返してもらうという考えです。

cycles.en_text_before_rewrite:
# The AI Phone Call Had a Human Helper

An AI called. That was what people thought as they spoke. But a human appeared from behind the scenes. A test involving Muse, Meta’s AI agent, became a reveal of what was really happening.

### The human backup plan

Through Muse, trained human contract workers made some calls and completed the exchanges with users. The idea was practical: when AI struggled, a person could help. Keeping a human in reserve seemed safer than leaving everything to AI.

But that backup plan changed the meaning of the call.

### The hidden cost of a smooth call

The test began without properly telling people what was happening. So people who thought they were speaking with AI were actually speaking with human staff. These workers did more than make the conversation smooth: the user’s sensitive information might be shared with contract workers at a call center. One helper meant one more person handling private data.

This is the interesting, slightly frightening turn. People often worry that an AI phone call will produce a strange answer. Here, the opposite happened. The voice was not simply human-like; a human was really speaking. And people were not properly told.

In response, a Meta executive admitted that starting a test in which contract workers made calls without properly telling people was a mistake. The human concierge feature was then rolled back for the time being.

AI stories usually focus on machines moving closer to people. Muse asks a different question: if humans enter AI’s backstage, can users be told? Who is speaking, and who can see the information?

## In one line

Unless both facts are explained at the start, a service of the future can quickly look like a call from a stranger.

AIの電話、その正体は人間の助っ人でした

AIから電話が来た。そう思って話していたら、舞台裏から登場したのは人間だった。MetaのAIエージェント、Museをめぐって、そんな種明かしのようなテストが行われていました。

Museを通じた電話の一部では、AIではなく、訓練を受けた人間の契約スタッフが電話をかけ、相手とのやり取りを完了させていました。

AIが苦手な場面で人間が助ける。仕組みだけ見れば、かなり現実的な作戦です。AIに全部任せるより、人間を控えに置くほうが安心。そんな発想だったのかもしれません。

ところが電話は、ここで一気にややこしくなります。適切な開示がないままテストが始まったため、相手から見ると、AIの電話のはずが、人間のスタッフと話していることになります。

しかも、その人間スタッフは、会話をなめらかにするだけではありません。電話を担当すれば、ユーザーの機微な情報が、コールセンターの契約スタッフに共有される可能性があります。

AIに人間の助っ人を一人入れたら、情報を扱う人も増える。便利さの裏から、プライバシーの問題が顔を出したわけです。

ここが今回の、面白くて少し怖いところです。AIの電話で心配されがちなのは、機械が変な答えを返すことですよね。でも今回は逆でした。話し方が人間らしすぎたのではなく、本当に人間が話していた。しかも、そのことが十分に知らされていませんでした。

この問題を受け、Metaの幹部は、適切な開示なしに契約スタッフが電話をかけるテストを始めたのはミスだったと認めました。そして、人間が対応するコンシェルジュ機能を当面ロールバックしました。

AIの世界では、機械が人間に近づく話ばかりが注目されます。今回のMuseは、そこに別の問いを持ち込みました。人間がAIの裏側に入るなら、その事実を利用者に伝えられるのか。誰が話しているのか。誰が情報を見るのか。

電話では、その二つを最初に説明しないと、未来のサービスが一瞬で、知らない人からの電話に見えてしまうのです。

# It Was Supposed to Be an AI Call, but a Human Appeared Behind the Scenes

Ask AI to make a haircut appointment. Have it call a store, ask about an item’s stock, and get an estimate from a supplier. The AI on your screen does all of it. It is a very convenient future.

Meta’s AI agent, Muse, actually has phone features like these.

But something unexpected happened behind the scenes. In some calls made through Muse, the caller was not AI but trained contract workers.

Muse receives the request. Up to that point, it is AI. But then it hands the task over to human staff. The staff make the call and finish the conversation. It was as if a supporting actor, hard to spot in the script, had appeared in a play starring AI.

This system was called “human concierges.” The fact that humans handled the calls was not, by itself, an immediate problem. The bigger problem was that testing began without giving people enough information about this fact.

Meta employees raised concerns that sensitive user information needed for the calls might be shared by mistake with contracted call-center workers.

This is an important point. There was no confirmation that a large-scale information leak had taken place. But people did not know who was actually handling the work they had asked AI to do. Also, their personal information might reach that person. When that happens, a convenient service suddenly starts to look like a mystery story.

Meta executives admitted that starting the test without a proper explanation was a mistake. They also temporarily put back the feature in which humans handled the calls. They did not stop Muse itself.

Going forward, Meta plans to make the feature available only when preparations are complete and it can clearly explain who will make the calls.

Even in an age when AI does our work, humans may step in to help. But when they do, they should not appear secretly. If they step onto the stage, they should say who they are first. This incident showed that simple rule in a very memorable way.

これ、ちょっと面白くない？　トランプ氏が新しい負担を打ち出したのに、取り下げても原油価格がほとんど下がらなかった。

7月13日、トランプ氏は、米国がホルムズ海峡の安全を守る費用として、海峡を通るすべての貨物に20％を求めると発表した。ホルムズ海峡は、中東から原油を運ぶ船が多く通る重要な海の道だ。そこに大きな料金をかける、という案だった。

ところが翌14日、トランプ氏はこの20％案をやめると発表した。代わりに、湾岸諸国が米国との貿易や投資を増やす形にするという。中東の指導者たちと「非常に生産的な協議」をしたことが、判断の背景にあると説明した。

普通なら、負担がなくなれば「では原油価格も下がるのでは」と思う。実際、発表の直後には、代表的な原油価格であるBrent先物の上げ幅が少し縮まった。

しかし、その動きは長く続かなかった。Brent先物はすぐに、発表前に近い高い水準へ戻った。報道時点では約2.6％高で、1バレル85ドルを超えていた。

ここで大事なのは、市場が見ているものだ。投資家が気にしているのは、20％の料金案が残るかどうかだけではない。米国とイランの間で攻撃が続いていること、海が封鎖される心配があること、タンカーが安全に航行できるか不安が残っていることだ。

つまり、料金案は消えても、海そのものの危険は消えていない。市場から見ると、「請求書の形」は変わっても、「原油を運べるのか」という問題はそのままなのだ。

遠い中東の海の話に見えるが、原油価格が高い状態が続けば、ガソリンや輸送費など、私たちの身近な価格にも影響する。今回の動きは、ニュースの見出しが変わっても、現実のリスクが残れば市場は簡単には安心しない、ということをよく示している。

# 20% Withdrawn—but the Oil Chart Was Not Finished Yet

This news feels like a short play in three acts. Act One was “20%.” Act Two brought an unexpected turn. Act Three was an unexpected move in oil prices.

The curtain rose on July 13. Trump posted that the United States would seek a 20% charge on all cargo passing through the Strait of Hormuz. The aim was to recover the cost of US efforts to keep the strait safe.

But “20%” was not a finished system. The post did not say who would pay, how the money would be collected, or what legal basis would support it. For the moment, only a large number stood at center stage.

The number stayed at center stage for about a day. Then the story took a sharp turn.

### The 20% plan changes overnight

The next day, Trump said the 20% plan would be replaced by trade and investment projects between Gulf states and the US. He cited “very productive discussions” with Middle Eastern leaders. He also said no one should charge ships in the strait, and that he disliked fees.

The change was sudden. But to read the oil move, the dates must be kept separate. On July 13, Brent rose about 10% and settled at about $83 a barrel. The rise was linked to concern about a US sea blockade of Iran, planned for the next day, and energy shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.

### The chart refuses to stay down

On July 14, after the withdrawal and replacement announcement, Brent crude futures briefly gave back some of their gains. Soon, they returned close to the high level before the announcement. At the time of reporting, Brent was up about 3%, above $85 a barrel. Its final settlement price was about $85, up about 2% from the day before.

## In one line

Concerns about US-Iran attacks, the sea blockade, and tanker safety continued on July 14, so the flashy 20% plan left the stage, but the chart only pulled back briefly before recovering: the policy turn and the oil chart’s “not over yet” movement happened on the same day.

cycles.en_text_before_rewrite:
# I Thought It Was an AI Call—But There Was a Person Inside? Meta’s Unexpected Muse Test

Ring, ring... A call came from an AI agent. That was what it seemed. But while the conversation continued, the voice on the other end was not AI. It was a person.

Meta had run a test that produced exactly this kind of surprise.

The setting was the phone feature of Muse, an AI agent. In some calls made through Muse, trained contract workers, not AI, made the calls and carried the conversations through to the end.

It was like an AI costume: take it off, and a person steps out. Of course, having a person handle a call is not automatically bad. A person can take over when AI alone has trouble. As a system, that may even seem useful.

But then a problem appeared.

### What Callers Were Not Told

When contract workers handled calls, sensitive user information could be shared with call-center staff. People feel differently when they think they are speaking to a machine and when they know a person is listening. Names, plans, and private matters are easier to share when you know who is hearing them. The test began without explaining that contract staff might call.

This was where the story changed.

### The Reveal Behind the AI Sign

The reveal was not AI learning to sound human. A human was behind the AI sign. As AI makes calls and reservations, useful features make people want to know whether AI or a person is on the other end. A Meta executive called the undisclosed test a “mistake,” and the “human concierge” feature was rolled back for now.

## In one line

In the AI age, making a voice sound human is not enough: people must first be told who is on the other end.

AIからの電話だと思ったら…中に“人”がいた？　MetaのMuseで起きたまさかの展開

プルルル……。AIエージェントから電話がかかってきた。そう思って話していたら、電話の向こうにいたのはAIではなく、人間だった――。

そんな展開を思わせるテストを、Metaが行っていました。

舞台は、AIエージェント「Muse」の電話機能です。Muse経由の電話の一部で、AIではなく、訓練を受けた人間の契約スタッフが電話をかけ、相手とのやり取りを最後まで進めていました。

AIが電話をしていると思ったら、実は人間が話している。まるで、AIの着ぐるみを脱いだら中から人が出てくるような話です。

もちろん、人間が対応すること自体が悪いわけではありません。AIだけでは難しい場面を、人が引き継ぐ。仕組みとしては、むしろ便利そうです。

しかし、ここで問題が起きました。

人間のスタッフが電話を担当すると、利用者の機微な情報が、コールセンターの契約スタッフに共有される可能性があります。

「機械に話している」と思って伝えるのと、「人が聞いている」と知って話すのでは、安心感が違います。名前や予定、個人的な事情などを話すとき、相手が誰なのかは大事な情報です。

しかも今回は、契約スタッフが電話をかけることについて、適切な説明が十分にないままテストが始まりました。利用者にはAIとのやり取りに見えても、実際には人間が関わっている場合があったのです。

ここが今回の“種明かし”です。AIが人間のように話したのではありません。人間が、AIの看板の後ろにいた。未来っぽい話なのに、問題の中心にあるのは「誰が電話しているのかを、ちゃんと伝えたのか」という、とても基本的なことでした。

AIが電話や予約を代わりにしてくれるほど、この確認は身近になります。便利な機能ほど、相手がAIなのか、人間なのかを知りたくなるからです。

Metaの幹部は、適切な開示なしにこのテストを始めたことを「ミス」と認めました。そして、人間のコンシェルジュ機能は当面ロールバックされました。

AIの時代に必要なのは、声を人間らしくする技術だけではありません。電話の向こうに誰がいるのかを、最初に教えること。Museの一件は、その大事なルールを、かなりドラマチックに見せてくれました。

一部のAI電話、舞台裏に人間がいた

ちょっとしたどんでん返しです。AIに電話を頼めるサービスの舞台裏で、電話をかけていたのが人間だった。そんなテストが行われていました。

主役は、MetaのAIエージェント、Museです。Museには、米国内の企業や店に電話して、散髪の予約を取ったり、在庫を確認したり、業者から見積もりを取ったりする機能があります。面倒な電話をAIに任せられるなら、かなり便利そうです。

ところが、電話機能の一部のテストでは、AIではなく、訓練を受けた人間の契約スタッフが電話をかけていました。そして、相手とのやり取りを最後まで終えていたのです。

ここで問題になったのは、人間が電話をしたこと自体ではありません。誰が話しているのかを、利用者にどう伝えるかです。

Museに電話を頼んだ利用者は、AIが電話をしていると考えるかもしれません。けれど、その一部では人間が話していた。しかも、適切な説明がないままなら、利用者は相手がAIなのか人間なのかを知ることができません。AIの便利さを楽しんでいたら、いつの間にか電話の向こうに人間がいた。そんな舞台裏です。

さらに、電話を進めるために利用者の情報が必要になる場合、その情報がコールセンターの契約スタッフに意図せず共有される可能性もあります。Metaの従業員は、この点をプライバシー上の懸念として社内で示しました。

報道では、インターネットやケーブル料金を交渉する電話で、人間のスタッフによる人種に関する不適切な発言があったという従業員の報告も紹介されています。ただし、これは一件の報告です。契約スタッフ全体の話に広げることはできません。

Metaの幹部は、適切な開示なしにこのテストを始めたのはミスだったと認めました。そして、人間コンシェルジュ機能を当面、以前の状態に戻しました。

AI電話の本当の難所は、話し方だけではありません。電話の向こうに誰がいるのかを、正直に伝えられるかどうかです。便利なサービスほど、舞台裏の出演者を隠してはいけない。Museの一件は、そんな当たり前で大事なことを見せてくれました。

# The Fee Plan Leaves, High Oil Prices Stay

On July 13, a plan suddenly appeared to charge a 20 percent fee on cargo passing through the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump said the fee was meant to recover the cost of the United States keeping the strait safe. It would cover all cargo passing through the strait. But important details—such as who would collect the fee, who would pay it, and how it would be calculated—were still blank.

In other words, fee collection had not actually begun. What appeared on stage was not a finished fee system, but a proposal that put forward the number 20 percent.

Then, the next day, the story suddenly changed. Trump announced that he would drop the 20 percent fee plan and replace it with trade and investment deals between Gulf countries and the United States. He explained that the decision was based on “very productive talks” with Middle Eastern leaders.

He also told reporters that no one should charge fees to ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz, and that he did not like the idea of fees itself. The 20 percent plan left the stage about one day after it appeared.

Now, let us turn the camera toward the oil market. The next scene begins.

After the withdrawal and replacement of the fee plan were announced, Brent crude oil futures briefly gave up some of their gains. Just when it seemed that prices might start to fall, they soon returned to a high level close to where they had been before the announcement. At the time of reporting, they were up about 2.6 percent, above 85 dollars a barrel.

What we can see here is that oil prices did not fall across the board immediately after the plan was withdrawn. At the same time, attacks by the United States and Iran, a sea blockade, and concerns about tanker safety continued.

The fee plan disappeared. But news about tensions around the strait remained on stage. Even though political statements changed greatly, oil prices moved briefly and then returned to a high level. What is interesting this time is that it seemed one headline alone could not decide how the story would end.

## In one line
The fee plan vanished, but oil prices stayed high as tensions around the Strait of Hormuz continued.

料金案は退場、原油高は居残り

七月十三日、いきなり登場したのは、ホルムズ海峡の貨物に二割を求めるという料金案でした。

トランプ氏が示した名目は、アメリカが海峡の安全を守る費用を返してもらうことです。対象は、海峡を通るすべての貨物。ところが、誰が集めるのか、誰が払うのか、どう計算するのかといった大事な部分は、まだ空欄でした。

つまり、実際に料金を徴収し始めたわけではありません。舞台に登場したのは、完成した料金制度ではなく、二割という数字を掲げた提案でした。

そして翌日、物語は急展開します。トランプ氏は、この二割の償還料案を取りやめ、湾岸諸国によるアメリカ向けの貿易や投資の案件に置き換えると発表しました。中東の指導者たちとの「非常に生産的な協議」に基づく決定だと説明しています。

さらに記者団には、ホルムズ海峡を通る船に誰も料金を課すべきではない、料金という考え方自体を好まないとも話しました。二割案は、登場から約一日で舞台を降りたことになります。

ここで原油市場にカメラを向けると、次の場面が始まります。

料金案の撤回と置き換えが発表されたあと、ブレント原油先物は上げ幅を一時的に縮めました。これで値下がりの幕が開くのかと思ったところ、ほどなくして、発表前に近い高い水準へ戻りました。報道時点では約二点六パーセント高で、一バレル八十五ドルを超えていました。

このとき確認できるのは、撤回の直後に原油価格が全面的に下落したわけではない、ということです。同じ時間帯には、アメリカとイランの攻撃、海上封鎖、タンカーの安全への懸念が続いていました。

料金案は消えました。けれど、海峡をめぐる緊張に関するニュースは、舞台に残ったままです。政治の発言が大きく変わっても、原油価格は一度揺れたあと、高い水準へ戻った。今回の面白さは、まるで一つの見出しだけでは、物語の結末まで決められなかったように見えるところです。

# The Oil Market's Main Player: The 20% Bill That Disappeared

This news may make Mr. Trump look like the main player. But the most interesting move came from oil, which did not fall in price.

On July 13, Mr. Trump proposed charging all cargo passing through the Strait of Hormuz a 20 percent “reimbursement fee.” Simply put, the plan was to make cargo passing through the strait help pay the cost of keeping it safe, a bit like handing a large bill to all cargo passing through the strait.

The next day, however, the scene suddenly changed. Mr. Trump withdrew the 20 percent plan and announced that it would instead be replaced by trade and investment deals between the Gulf states and the United States. He explained that this followed “very productive talks” with Middle Eastern leaders.

A plan to charge a fee directly had changed into a discussion of trade and investment. It seemed as if the rough waves had become a little calmer. The oil market also reacted once, right after the announcement.

Brent crude oil futures narrowed their gains after the announcement. But that calm did not last long. The price soon returned to a high level close to where it had been before the announcement. At the time of reporting, it was above 85 dollars a barrel.

It was as if oil had replied, “I understand that the bill is gone. But that alone is not enough to feel safe.”

Of course, oil cannot speak. But its price movement seemed to show that people were watching not only whether there was a fee plan, but also the danger of the strait itself.

Attacks continue between the United States and Iran. Concerns about a blockade at sea remain, and worries about whether tankers can pass safely have not gone away. Even after the plan was replaced by one about trade and investment, this part has not changed.

Even if this seems like a story about a distant sea, oil prices are linked to gasoline prices and transportation costs. This price movement was a scene that oil showed on its stage: even if politics changes the name of a plan, that does not mean the danger along the route has disappeared.

## In one line
Trump withdrew the proposed Strait of Hormuz fee, but oil prices stayed high because shipping risks remained.

# We Thought It Was AI—But There Was a Person Inside Meta’s Muse

Ring, ring. A call seemed to come from an AI agent. But as the conversation went on, the voice was not AI at all. It was a person.

Meta had run a test that caused exactly this surprise.

The test used the phone feature of its AI agent, Muse. In some calls through Muse, trained contract workers made the calls, not AI. They carried each conversation through to the end.

It was like someone took off an AI costume. Then a person stepped out.

Having a person take over is not always a bad thing. A human can handle situations that AI alone finds difficult. As a system, this may even be useful.

But this was where the problem began. A human staff member might handle the call. Then the user’s sensitive information could be shared with a contract worker at a call center.

It is one thing to speak because you think a machine is listening. It is another when you know a person is listening. When people share their names, plans, or personal situations, it matters who listens.

### The hidden person behind the AI sign

Here was the reveal. The test began without clearly telling users that contract workers would make the calls. A user might think the exchange was with AI, even though a person was involved.

AI had not learned to speak like a human. A human stood behind the sign that said AI.

It seemed like a story from the future. But the main question was very basic: Had users been clearly told who was making the call?

As AI becomes able to make calls or reservations for us, this question will become more familiar. The more useful the feature, the more people will want to know who is on the other side. They will want to know if it is AI or human.

### Meta admits a mistake

A Meta executive admitted the mistake. The test had begun without clearly telling users.

For now, Meta has pulled back the human concierge feature. In the AI age, technology that makes a voice sound human is not enough. We must also know, at the start, who is on the other end.

## In one line

Before AI speaks for us, we need to know whether the voice belongs to AI or a person.

# Some AI Phone Calls Had Humans Behind the Scenes

There was a small twist. A service let people ask AI to make phone calls. But humans were making some calls behind the scenes. This was part of a test.

The main service was Muse, Meta’s AI assistant. Muse can call businesses and stores in the United States. It can book haircuts, check if items are in stock, and ask for price estimates. If AI can handle difficult phone calls, it seems very useful.

But in some tests of its calling feature, trained human contract workers made the calls instead of AI. They spoke with people until each conversation ended.

The problem was not that humans made the calls. The problem was how users were told who was speaking.

People who asked Muse to make a call might think AI was doing it. But sometimes, a human was speaking instead. If this was not explained clearly, users could not know if it was AI or a person. They enjoyed the ease of AI. But they did not know that a human was on the other end. This was happening behind the scenes.

Also, a call might need user information to continue. That information might then be shared by mistake with contract workers at a call center. Meta employees raised this inside the company as a privacy concern.

News reports also quoted a report from an employee. It said that human staff made inappropriate comments about race during calls to bargain over internet or cable fees. However, this is only one report. It would be wrong to say this about all contract workers.

Some calls through Meta’s AI assistant were handled by humans, but users were not properly told.

# The 20 Percent Fee Plan Is Withdrawn—But Oil Prices Quickly Return

Oil-price news sometimes gets its biggest twist not from a policy announcement, but from what prices do after it. This time, the fee plan left the stage, but the price did not leave with it.

### The proposed fee enters, then exits

On July 13, Trump posted that all cargo passing through the Strait of Hormuz should provide a 20 percent reimbursement. A large number suddenly appeared, making the proposal the story’s new lead. But the next day, July 14, he posted that the 20 percent fee would be replaced by trade and investment deals between Gulf states and the United States.

### The price refuses to follow

Trump said the change was based on “very productive discussions” with Middle Eastern leaders. He also told reporters that no one should charge ships using the Strait of Hormuz, and said he did not like the idea of a fee itself. Normally, removing the fee plan would seem likely to calm oil prices. Brent futures briefly narrowed their gains, but soon returned to near their earlier high.

That return is the interesting part. On the political stage, the sign above the entrance was changed. But on the price stage, the numbers quickly regained their earlier strength. At the time of publication, oil was up about 2.6 percent and above $85 a barrel.

During that period, attacks between the United States and Iran, a sea blockade, and concerns about tanker safety continued.

The lesson is that changing the words in an announcement does not always change the price in the same way. The fee plan may be replaced, but events continuing at the same time do not simply disappear backstage because of one announcement.

## In one line

The fee plan left the stage, but the events driving oil prices—and the prices themselves—quickly returned.

stage2_results.local_context:
# It Was Supposed to Be an AI Call—Then a Human Appeared Backstage

Imagine asking AI to book a haircut. Or asking it to call a store and check whether something is in stock. It could even ask a supplier for a price estimate. In this convenient future, the AI on your screen handles everything for you.

Meta’s AI agent, Muse, really does have phone features like these. So it sounds like a simple story: you make a request, and AI takes care of the call. But the picture changed once people looked behind the stage.

### The call that was not made by AI

Some calls through Muse were not made by AI at all. Trained human contract workers made them. Muse received the request—that part was AI—but then passed the job to a person. The worker made the call and finished the conversation. It was like an AI-led play with a hidden supporting actor. The system was called “human concierges.”

The hidden role made the simple picture less simple.

### Why the hidden role mattered

Meta employees worried that sensitive information needed for the calls might be shared by mistake with contract workers at a call center. The issue was not that humans handled calls. It was that testing began without clearly telling users about it. A service that seemed simple now looked like a mystery story.

No large information leak was confirmed. But users could not know who was really doing the work they had asked AI to do—and their personal information might reach that person. That uncertainty turned convenience into a mystery.

A Meta executive admitted that starting the test without a proper explanation was a mistake. Meta then temporarily put the human-call feature back on hold. The company did not stop Muse itself.

In the future, Meta will make the feature public only when it is ready and can clearly explain who will make the call.

Even in an age when AI does our work, a human may still need to help. But that person should not appear secretly. If they step onto the stage, they should give their name first. This case made that simple rule unusually clear.

## In one line

AI may need human help, but humans must say clearly when they take over.

二十パーセントは退場した。それでも原油の不安は残った

原油市場で、主役が一日で交代しました。最初に登場したのは、ホルムズ海峡を通る貨物への二十パーセントの償還料です。ところが翌日、この案は舞台から消えました。普通なら、原油価格もひと安心しそうです。

しかし、原油市場の反応は少し違いました。料金案が消えた直後に、価格は下がりかけました。ところがすぐに、高い水準へ戻ったのです。まるで市場が、「料金の話は終わっても、海峡の話は終わっていません」と見ていたようでした。

始まりは七月十三日です。トランプ氏は、ホルムズ海峡を通るすべての貨物に、二十パーセントを求める案を示しました。アメリカが海峡の安全を守るために使う費用を、貨物を運ぶ側に返してもらうという考えです。

海峡を通る荷物に、大きな料金が突然かかるかもしれない。原油もこの海峡を通るため、輸送に影響が出れば、価格が上がる可能性があります。市場が身構えたのは、このためです。

ところが七月十四日、トランプ氏は二十パーセント案を、湾岸諸国がアメリカと進める貿易や投資の案件に置き換えると発表しました。中東の指導者たちとの「非常に生産的な協議」が背景にあると説明しました。

ここで料金案は退場です。発表後、ブレント原油先物の上げ幅は一時縮まりました。ところが、ほどなく発表前に近い高い水準へ戻りました。報道時点では、一バレル八十五ドルを超え、約二・六パーセント高でした。

なぜ下がり切らなかったのでしょうか。市場が見ていたのは、料金の有無だけではなかったからです。米国とイランの間では攻撃が続き、海上封鎖の懸念もあります。タンカーが安全に進めるのかという不安も消えていません。

つまり、退場したのは料金案であって、海峡の危険ではありません。発表は一日で変わっても、船が安全に通れるかという現実は変わらない。原油市場の本当の主役は、料金ではなく、危険な航路そのものだったのです。遠い海峡の不安は、原油を通じてガソリンや物流の値段にもつながります。

# The AI Phone Call Had a Human Helper

An AI called. That was what people thought as they spoke. But a human appeared from behind the scenes. A test involving Muse, Meta’s AI agent, became a reveal of what was really happening.

### The human backup plan

Through Muse, trained human contract workers made some calls and completed the exchanges with users. The idea was practical: when AI struggled, a person could help. Keeping a human in reserve seemed safer than leaving everything to AI.

But that backup plan changed the meaning of the call.

### The hidden cost of a smooth call

The test began without properly telling people what was happening. So people who thought they were speaking with AI were actually speaking with human staff. These workers did more than make the conversation smooth: the user’s sensitive information might be shared with contract workers at a call center. One helper meant one more person handling private data.

This is the interesting, slightly frightening turn. People often worry that an AI phone call will produce a strange answer. Here, the opposite happened. The voice was not simply human-like; a human was really speaking. And people were not properly told.

In response, a Meta executive admitted that starting a test in which contract workers made calls without properly telling people was a mistake. The human concierge feature was then rolled back for the time being.

AI stories usually focus on machines moving closer to people. Muse asks a different question: if humans enter AI’s backstage, can users be told? Who is speaking, and who can see the information?

## In one line

Unless both facts are explained at the start, a service of the future can quickly look like a call from a stranger.

AIの電話、その正体は人間の助っ人でした

AIから電話が来た。そう思って話していたら、舞台裏から登場したのは人間だった。MetaのAIエージェント、Museをめぐって、そんな種明かしのようなテストが行われていました。

Museを通じた電話の一部では、AIではなく、訓練を受けた人間の契約スタッフが電話をかけ、相手とのやり取りを完了させていました。

AIが苦手な場面で人間が助ける。仕組みだけ見れば、かなり現実的な作戦です。AIに全部任せるより、人間を控えに置くほうが安心。そんな発想だったのかもしれません。

ところが電話は、ここで一気にややこしくなります。適切な開示がないままテストが始まったため、相手から見ると、AIの電話のはずが、人間のスタッフと話していることになります。

しかも、その人間スタッフは、会話をなめらかにするだけではありません。電話を担当すれば、ユーザーの機微な情報が、コールセンターの契約スタッフに共有される可能性があります。

AIに人間の助っ人を一人入れたら、情報を扱う人も増える。便利さの裏から、プライバシーの問題が顔を出したわけです。

ここが今回の、面白くて少し怖いところです。AIの電話で心配されがちなのは、機械が変な答えを返すことですよね。でも今回は逆でした。話し方が人間らしすぎたのではなく、本当に人間が話していた。しかも、そのことが十分に知らされていませんでした。

この問題を受け、Metaの幹部は、適切な開示なしに契約スタッフが電話をかけるテストを始めたのはミスだったと認めました。そして、人間が対応するコンシェルジュ機能を当面ロールバックしました。

AIの世界では、機械が人間に近づく話ばかりが注目されます。今回のMuseは、そこに別の問いを持ち込みました。人間がAIの裏側に入るなら、その事実を利用者に伝えられるのか。誰が話しているのか。誰が情報を見るのか。

電話では、その二つを最初に説明しないと、未来のサービスが一瞬で、知らない人からの電話に見えてしまうのです。

# The AI Phone Call Had a Human Helper

An AI called. That was what people thought as they spoke. But a human appeared from behind the scenes. A test involving Muse, Meta’s AI agent, became a reveal of what was really happening.

### The human backup plan

Through Muse, trained human contract workers made some calls and completed the exchanges. The idea was practical: when AI struggled, a person could help. Keeping a human in reserve seemed safer than leaving everything to AI.

But that backup plan changed the meaning of the call.

### The hidden cost of a smooth call

The test began without properly telling people what was happening. So contract staff handled some calls in a test without proper disclosure. These workers did more than make the conversation smooth: the user’s sensitive information might be shared with contract workers at a call center. One helper meant one more person handling private data.

This is the interesting, slightly frightening turn. People often worry that an AI phone call will produce a strange answer. Here, the opposite happened. The voice was not simply human-like; a human was really speaking. And people were not properly told.

In response, a Meta executive admitted that starting a test in which contract workers made calls without properly telling people was a mistake. The human concierge feature was then rolled back for the time being.

AI stories usually focus on machines moving closer to people. Muse asks a different question: if humans enter AI’s backstage, can users be told? Who is speaking, and who can see the information?

## In one line

Unless both facts are explained at the start, a service of the future can quickly look like a call from a stranger.

AIの電話、その正体は人間の助っ人でした

AIから電話が来た。そう思って話していたら、舞台裏から登場したのは人間だった。MetaのAIエージェント、Museをめぐって、そんな種明かしのようなテストが行われていました。

Museを通じた電話の一部では、AIではなく、訓練を受けた人間の契約スタッフが電話をかけ、相手とのやり取りを完了させていました。

AIが苦手な場面で人間が助ける。仕組みだけ見れば、かなり現実的な作戦です。AIに全部任せるより、人間を控えに置くほうが安心。そんな発想だったのかもしれません。

ところが電話は、ここで一気にややこしくなります。適切な開示がないままテストが始まったため、相手から見ると、AIの電話のはずが、人間のスタッフと話していることになります。

しかも、その人間スタッフは、会話をなめらかにするだけではありません。電話を担当すれば、ユーザーの機微な情報が、コールセンターの契約スタッフに共有される可能性があります。

AIに人間の助っ人を一人入れたら、情報を扱う人も増える。便利さの裏から、プライバシーの問題が顔を出したわけです。

ここが今回の、面白くて少し怖いところです。AIの電話で心配されがちなのは、機械が変な答えを返すことですよね。でも今回は逆でした。話し方が人間らしすぎたのではなく、本当に人間が話していた。しかも、そのことが十分に知らされていませんでした。

この問題を受け、Metaの幹部は、適切な開示なしに契約スタッフが電話を担当するテストを始めたのはミスだったと認めました。そして、人間が対応するコンシェルジュ機能を当面ロールバックしました。

AIの世界では、機械が人間に近づく話ばかりが注目されます。今回のMuseは、そこに別の問いを持ち込みました。人間がAIの裏側に入るなら、その事実を利用者に伝えられるのか。誰が話しているのか。誰が情報を見るのか。

電話では、その二つを最初に説明しないと、未来のサービスが一瞬で、知らない人からの電話に見えてしまうのです。

# It Was Supposed to Be an AI Call, but a Human Appeared Behind the Scenes

Ask AI to make a haircut appointment. Have it call a store, ask about an item’s stock, and get an estimate from a supplier. The AI on your screen does all of it. It is a very convenient future.

Meta’s AI agent, Muse, actually has phone features like these.

But something unexpected happened behind the scenes. In some calls made through Muse, the caller was not AI but trained contract workers.

Muse receives the request. Up to that point, it is AI. But then it hands the task over to human staff. The staff make the call and finish the conversation. It was as if a supporting actor, hard to spot in the script, had appeared in a play starring AI.

This system was called “human concierges.” The fact that humans handled the calls was not, by itself, an immediate problem. The bigger problem was that testing began without giving people enough information about this fact.

Meta employees raised concerns that sensitive user information needed for the calls might be shared by mistake with contracted call-center workers.

This is an important point. There was no confirmation that a large-scale information leak had taken place. But people did not know who was actually handling the work they had asked AI to do. Also, their personal information might reach that person. When that happens, a convenient service suddenly starts to look like a mystery story.

Meta executives admitted that starting the test without a proper explanation was a mistake. They also temporarily put back the feature in which humans handled the calls. They did not stop Muse itself.

Going forward, Meta plans to make the feature available only when preparations are complete and it can clearly explain who will make the calls.

Even in an age when AI does our work, humans may step in to help. But when they do, they should not appear secretly. If they step onto the stage, they should say who they are first. This incident showed that simple rule in a very memorable way.

7月13日、トランプ氏は、米国がホルムズ海峡の安全を守る費用として、海峡を通るすべての貨物に20％を求めると発表した。ホルムズ海峡は、中東から原油を運ぶ船が多く通る重要な海の道だ。そこに大きな料金をかける、という案だった。

ところが翌14日、トランプ氏はこの20％案をやめると発表した。代わりに、湾岸諸国が米国との貿易や投資を増やす形にするという。中東の指導者たちと「非常に生産的な協議」をしたことが、判断の背景にあると説明した。

# A Big Twist in the 20 Percent Fee, But Crude Oil Does Not Leave the Stage

This news story looks like a short drama if we look only at how it unfolded.

The first act came on July 13. Trump proposed a 20 percent fee on all cargo passing through the Strait of Hormuz. The stated reason was to recover the money the United States spends to keep the strait safe.

It looked like a very large fee would appear every time a ship passed through the strait. But no details were given about the system, such as who would pay or how the money would be collected. The fee was not actually being collected yet. It was still only at the stage of announcing the policy.

Then came the second act, just one day later.

Trump withdrew the 20 percent fee plan. In its place came trade and investment deals between Gulf countries and the United States. He explained that this followed “very productive talks” with leaders from the Middle East.

A story about charging ships suddenly changed into a story about trade and investment. It was as if the main actor had changed costumes—and roles—in the middle of the play.

Now for the third act: crude oil prices appeared.

When the replacement of the fee plan was announced, Brent crude futures briefly reduced their gains. But that move did not last long. Before long, they returned to a high level close to where they had been before the announcement. When the article appeared, they were up about 2.6 percent, at more than 85 dollars a barrel.

The disappearance of the fee plan did not lead to a large, lasting fall in prices. Attacks between the United States and Iran continued, and concerns about a sea blockade and the safety of tankers remained.

Of course, this price movement alone cannot tell us that there was just one reason for the price. But even after the fee plan left the stage, other factors remained on that same stage. So the price reacted once, then returned to a high level. What made this news interesting was that even when the sign on the news changed, the whole stage did not change in an instant.

## In one line

# A Big Twist in the 20 Percent Fee, But Crude Oil Does Not Leave the Stage

This news story looks like a short drama if we look only at how it unfolded.

The first act came on July 13. Trump proposed a 20 percent fee on all cargo passing through the Strait of Hormuz. The stated reason was to recover the money the United States spends to keep the strait safe.

It looked like a very large fee would appear every time a ship passed through the strait. But no details were given about the system, such as who would pay or how the money would be collected. The fee was not actually being collected yet. It was still only at the stage of announcing the policy.

Then came the second act, just one day later.

Trump withdrew the 20 percent fee plan. In its place came trade and investment deals between Gulf countries and the United States. He explained that this followed “very productive talks” with leaders from the Middle East.

A story about charging ships suddenly changed into a story about trade and investment. It was as if the main actor had changed costumes—and roles—in the middle of the play.

Now for the third act: crude oil prices appeared.

When the replacement of the fee plan was announced, Brent crude futures briefly reduced their gains. But that move did not last long. This news feels like a short play in three acts. Act One was “20%.” Act Two brought an unexpected turn. Act Three was an unexpected move in oil prices.

# I Thought It Was an AI Call—But There Was a Person Inside? Meta’s Unexpected Muse Test

Ring, ring... A call came from an AI agent. That was what it seemed. But while the conversation continued, the voice on the other end was not AI. It was a person.

Meta had run a test that produced exactly this kind of surprise.

The setting was the phone feature of Muse, an AI agent. In some calls made through Muse, trained contract workers, not AI, made the calls and carried the conversations through to the end.

It was like an AI costume: take it off, and a person steps out. Of course, having a person handle a call is not automatically bad. A person can take over when AI alone has trouble. As a system, that may even seem useful.

But then a problem appeared.

### What Callers Were Not Told

When contract workers handled calls, sensitive user information could be shared with call-center staff. People feel differently when they think they are speaking to a machine and when they know a person is listening. Names, plans, and private matters are easier to share when you know who is hearing them. The test began without explaining that contract staff might call.

This was where the story changed.

### The Reveal Behind the AI Sign

The reveal was not AI learning to sound human. A human was behind the AI sign. As AI makes calls and reservations, useful features make people want to know whether AI or a person is on the other end. A Meta executive called the undisclosed test a “mistake,” and the “human concierge” feature was rolled back for now.

## In one line

In the AI age, making a voice sound human is not enough: people must first be told who is on the other end.

AIからの電話だと思ったら…中に“人”がいた？　MetaのMuseで起きたまさかの展開

プルルル……。AIエージェントから電話がかかってきた。そう思って話していたら、電話の向こうにいたのはAIではなく、人間だった――。

そんな展開を思わせるテストを、Metaが行っていました。

舞台は、AIエージェント「Muse」の電話機能です。Muse経由の電話の一部で、AIではなく、訓練を受けた人間の契約スタッフが電話をかけ、相手とのやり取りを最後まで進めていました。

AIが電話をしていると思ったら、実は人間が話している。まるで、AIの着ぐるみを脱いだら中から人が出てくるような話です。

もちろん、人間が対応すること自体が悪いわけではありません。AIだけでは難しい場面を、人が引き継ぐ。仕組みとしては、むしろ便利そうです。

しかし、ここで問題が起きました。

人間のスタッフが電話を担当すると、利用者の機微な情報が、コールセンターの契約スタッフに共有される可能性があります。

「機械に話している」と思って伝えるのと、「人が聞いている」と知って話すのでは、安心感が違います。名前や予定、個人的な事情などを話すとき、相手が誰なのかは大事な情報です。

しかも今回は、契約スタッフが電話をかけることについて、適切な説明が十分にないままテストが始まりました。利用者にはAIとのやり取りに見えても、実際には人間が関わっている場合があったのです。

ここが今回の“種明かし”です。AIが人間のように話したのではありません。人間が、AIの看板の後ろにいた。未来っぽい話なのに、問題の中心にあるのは「誰が電話しているのかを、ちゃんと伝えたのか」という、とても基本的なことでした。

AIが電話や予約を代わりにしてくれるほど、この確認は身近になります。便利な機能ほど、相手がAIなのか、人間なのかを知りたくなるからです。

Metaの幹部は、適切な開示なしにこのテストを始めたことを「ミス」と認めました。そして、人間のコンシェルジュ機能は当面ロールバックされました。

AIの時代に必要なのは、声を人間らしくする技術だけではありません。電話の向こうに誰がいるのかを、最初に教えること。Museの一件は、その大事なルールを、かなりドラマチックに見せてくれました。

一部のAI電話、舞台裏に人間がいた

ちょっとしたどんでん返しです。AIに電話を頼めるサービスの舞台裏で、電話をかけていたのが人間だった。そんなテストが行われていました。

主役は、MetaのAIエージェント、Museです。Museには、米国内の企業や店に電話して、散髪の予約を取ったり、在庫を確認したり、業者から見積もりを取ったりする機能があります。面倒な電話をAIに任せられるなら、かなり便利そうです。

ところが、電話機能の一部のテストでは、AIではなく、訓練を受けた人間の契約スタッフが電話をかけていました。そして、相手とのやり取りを最後まで終えていたのです。

ここで問題になったのは、人間が電話をしたこと自体ではありません。誰が話しているのかを、利用者にどう伝えるかです。

Museに電話を頼んだ利用者は、AIが電話をしていると考えるかもしれません。けれど、その一部では人間が話していた。しかも、適切な説明がないままなら、利用者は相手がAIなのか人間なのかを知ることができません。AIの便利さを楽しんでいたら、いつの間にか電話の向こうに人間がいた。そんな舞台裏です。

さらに、電話を進めるために利用者の情報が必要になる場合、その情報がコールセンターの契約スタッフに意図せず共有される可能性もあります。Metaの従業員は、この点をプライバシー上の懸念として社内で示しました。

報道では、インターネットやケーブル料金を交渉する電話で、人間のスタッフによる人種に関する不適切な発言があったという従業員の報告も紹介されています。ただし、これは一件の報告です。契約スタッフ全体の話に広げることはできません。

Metaの幹部は、適切な開示なしにこのテストを始めたのはミスだったと認めました。そして、人間コンシェルジュ機能を当面、以前の状態に戻しました。

AI電話の本当の難所は、話し方だけではありません。電話の向こうに誰がいるのかを、正直に伝えられるかどうかです。便利なサービスほど、舞台裏の出演者を隠してはいけない。Museの一件は、そんな当たり前で大事なことを見せてくれました。

stage2_results.local_context:
# The Fee Plan Leaves, High Oil Prices Stay

On July 13, a plan suddenly appeared to charge a 20 percent fee on cargo passing through the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump said the fee was meant to recover the cost of the United States keeping the strait safe. It would cover all cargo passing through the strait. But important details—such as who would collect the fee, who would pay it, and how it would be calculated—were still blank.

In other words, fee collection had not actually begun. What appeared on stage was not a finished fee system, but a proposal that put forward the number 20 percent.

Then, the next day, the story suddenly changed. Trump announced that he would drop the 20 percent fee plan and replace it with trade and investment deals between Gulf countries and the United States. He explained that the decision was based on “very productive talks” with Middle Eastern leaders.

He also told reporters that no one should charge fees to ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz, and that he did not like the idea of fees itself. The 20 percent plan left the stage about one day after it appeared.

Now, let us turn the camera toward the oil market. The next scene begins.

After the withdrawal and replacement of the fee plan were announced, Brent crude oil futures briefly gave up some of their gains. Just when it seemed that prices might start to fall, they soon returned to a high level close to where they had been before the announcement. At the time of reporting, they were up about 2.6 percent, above 85 dollars a barrel.

What we can see here is that oil prices did not fall across the board immediately after the plan was withdrawn. At the same time, attacks by the United States and Iran, a sea blockade, and concerns about tanker safety continued.

The fee plan disappeared. But news about tensions around the strait remained on stage. Even though political statements changed greatly, oil prices moved briefly and then returned to a high level. What is interesting this time is that it seemed one headline alone could not decide how the story would end.

## In one line
The fee plan vanished, but oil prices stayed high as tensions around the Strait of Hormuz continued.

# The Oil Market's Main Player: The 20% Bill That Disappeared

This news may make Mr. Trump look like the main player. But the most interesting move came from oil, which did not fall in price.

On July 13, Mr. Trump proposed charging all cargo passing through the Strait of Hormuz a 20 percent “reimbursement fee.” Simply put, the plan was to make cargo passing through the strait help pay the cost of keeping it safe, a bit like handing a large bill to all cargo passing through the strait.

The next day, however, the scene suddenly changed. Mr. Trump withdrew the 20 percent plan and announced that it would instead be replaced by trade and investment deals between the Gulf states and the United States. He explained that this followed “very productive talks” with Middle Eastern leaders.

A plan to charge a fee directly had changed into a discussion of trade and investment. It seemed as if the rough waves had become a little calmer. The oil market also reacted once, right after the announcement.

Brent crude oil futures narrowed their gains after the announcement. But that calm did not last long. The price soon returned to a high level close to where it had been before the announcement. At the time of reporting, it was above 85 dollars a barrel.

It was as if oil had replied, “I understand that the bill is gone. But that alone is not enough to feel safe.”

Of course, oil cannot speak. But its price movement seemed to show that people were watching not only whether there was a fee plan, but also the danger of the strait itself.

Attacks continue between the United States and Iran. Concerns about a blockade at sea remain, and worries about whether tankers can pass safely have not gone away. Even after the plan was replaced by one about trade and investment, this part has not changed.

Even if this seems like a story about a distant sea, oil prices are linked to gasoline prices and transportation costs. This price movement was a scene that oil showed on its stage: even if politics changes the name of a plan, that does not mean the danger along the route has disappeared.

## In one line
Trump withdrew the proposed Strait of Hormuz fee, but oil prices stayed high because shipping risks remained.

This news story looks like a short drama if we look only at how it unfolded.

The first act came on July 13. Trump proposed a 20 percent fee on all cargo passing through the Strait of Hormuz. The stated reason was to recover the money the United States spends to keep the strait safe.

Trump withdrew the 20 percent fee plan. In its place came trade and investment deals between Gulf countries and the United States. He explained that this followed “very productive talks” with leaders from the Middle East.

Before long, they returned to a high level close to where they had been before the announcement. When the article appeared, they were up about 2.6 percent, at more than 85 dollars a barrel.

The disappearance of the fee plan did not lead to a large, lasting fall in prices. Attacks between the United States and Iran continued, and concerns about a sea blockade and the safety of tankers remained.

Of course, this price movement alone cannot tell us that there was just one reason for the price. But even after the fee plan left the stage, other factors remained on that same stage. # We Thought It Was AI—But There Was a Person Inside Meta’s Muse

Ring, ring. A call seemed to come from an AI agent. But as the conversation went on, the voice was not AI at all. It was a person.

Meta had run a test that caused exactly this surprise.

The test used the phone feature of its AI agent, Muse. In some calls through Muse, trained contract workers made the calls, not AI. They carried each conversation through to the end.

It was like someone took off an AI costume. Then a person stepped out.

Having a person take over is not always a bad thing. A human can handle situations that AI alone finds difficult. As a system, this may even be useful.

But this was where the problem began. A human staff member might handle the call. Then the user’s sensitive information could be shared with a contract worker at a call center.

It is one thing to speak because you think a machine is listening. It is another when you know a person is listening. When people share their names, plans, or personal situations, it matters who listens.

### The hidden person behind the AI sign

# Some AI Phone Calls Had Humans Behind the Scenes

There was a small twist. A service let people ask AI to make phone calls. But humans were making some calls behind the scenes. This was part of a test.

The main service was Muse, Meta’s AI assistant. Muse can call businesses and stores in the United States. It can book haircuts, check if items are in stock, and ask for price estimates. If AI can handle difficult phone calls, it seems very useful.

But in some tests of its calling feature, trained human contract workers made the calls instead of AI. They spoke with people until each conversation ended.

The problem was not that humans made the calls. The problem was how users were told who was speaking.

People who asked Muse to make a call might think AI was doing it. But sometimes, a human was speaking instead. If this was not explained clearly, users could not know if it was AI or a person. They enjoyed the ease of AI. But they did not know that a human was on the other end. This was happening behind the scenes.

Also, a call might need user information to continue. That information might then be shared by mistake with contract workers at a call center. Meta employees raised this inside the company as a privacy concern.

News reports also quoted a report from an employee. It said that human staff made inappropriate comments about race during calls to bargain over internet or cable fees. However, this is only one report. It would be wrong to say this about all contract workers.

Some calls through Meta’s AI assistant were handled by humans, but users were not properly told.

# The 20 Percent Fee Plan Is Withdrawn—But Oil Prices Quickly Return

Oil-price news sometimes gets its biggest twist not from a policy announcement, but from what prices do after it. This time, the fee plan left the stage, but the price did not leave with it.

### The proposed fee enters, then exits

On July 13, Trump posted that all cargo passing through the Strait of Hormuz should provide a 20 percent reimbursement. A large number suddenly appeared, making the proposal the story’s new lead. But the next day, July 14, he posted that the 20 percent fee would be replaced by trade and investment deals between Gulf states and the United States.

### The price refuses to follow

Trump said the change was based on “very productive discussions” with Middle Eastern leaders. He also told reporters that no one should charge ships using the Strait of Hormuz, and said he did not like the idea of a fee itself. Normally, removing the fee plan would seem likely to calm oil prices. Brent futures briefly narrowed their gains, but soon returned to near their earlier high.

That return is the interesting part. On the political stage, the sign above the entrance was changed. But on the price stage, the numbers quickly regained their earlier strength. At the time of publication, oil was up about 2.6 percent and above $85 a barrel.

During that period, attacks between the United States and Iran, a sea blockade, and concerns about tanker safety continued.

The lesson is that changing the words in an announcement does not always change the price in the same way. The fee plan may be replaced, but events continuing at the same time do not simply disappear backstage because of one announcement.

## In one line

The fee plan left the stage, but the events driving oil prices—and the prices themselves—quickly returned.

# Bags Split the Job: Mini Bags Catch the Eye, Large Bags Carry the Load

In 2026 fashion, mini bags are having a big moment. Palm-sized clutches, small pouches, and eye-catching minaudières fill runways and fashion reports. Some are so small that you might ask, “Can you really fit anything in that?”

But mini bags are not taking over. They are not pushing large bags away. In 2026, the two sizes seem to have different jobs. One carries what we need. The other helps create the look.

### ELLE’s small-bag examples

ELLE included mini bags among its fall and winter 2026 style trends. Its examples included Khaite’s palm-sized evening clutch and Chanel’s novelty minaudière. They mostly hold the basics: a phone, wallet, keys, and lip products. They cannot compete with roomy bags for storage. Their job is visual. They add a special feeling. They say, “This is today’s mood.”

We see the season more clearly by looking at bags beside them.

### Vogue’s wider list of bags

Vogue also covered the 2026 season. It showed small pouches from Prada and Loewe. It also showed Celine’s Ultra Maxi and Altuzarra’s large shoulder bag. It showed roomy totes from Toteme and other brands, too.

This list matters. Large bags had not disappeared. Small and large bags appeared in the same season.

We are not seeing mini bags spread through the whole market. Instead, they are back in fashion reports and on certain runways. Even so, trends now look different. Bags no longer play a game with only one size on the throne. Large bags are the luggage crew. They carry what we need. Mini bags are the stage crew. They catch the eye and set the mood. In 2026, the runway proudly shows this split in their work.

## In one line

In 2026, large bags carry the load, while mini bags carry the mood.

No large information leak was confirmed. But users could not know who was really doing the work they had asked AI to do—and their personal information might reach that person. That uncertainty turned convenience into a mystery.

A Meta executive admitted that starting the test without a proper explanation was a mistake. Meta then temporarily put the human-call feature back on hold. The company did not stop Muse itself.

In the future, Meta will make the feature public only when it is ready and can clearly explain who will make the call.

Even in an age when AI does our work, a human may still need to help. But that person should not appear secretly. If they step onto the stage, they should give their name first. This case made that simple rule unusually clear.

## In one line

AI may need human help, but humans must say clearly when they take over.
